About me

Every year, undetected plant pathogens destroy nearly 40% of the world’s crops, often before they are even identified. The challenge is not simply a lack of pesticides, but a lack of precision. As climate change accelerates pathogen evolution, conventional diagnostic systems are struggling to keep pace. My work focuses on addressing this problem at the molecular level.
I am Mahmud Sindid Ikram, a Molecular Plant Pathologist, Graduate Research Assistant at Bangladesh Agricultural University, and an MS candidate in Plant Pathology. My research integrates molecular diagnostics, pathogen biology, and applied disease management to improve the accuracy and efficiency of plant disease detection and control.
I work extensively with PCR, DNA barcoding, gel documentation, and NCBI BLAST to generate precise genetic data that supports real diagnostic decision-making. My experience spans the full research pipeline, from pathogen isolation and culture preparation to field experimentation and pathogenicity testing under real agricultural conditions.
Alongside molecular diagnostics, I evaluate Biological Control Agents as sustainable alternatives to chemical-dependent disease management. I also apply R Studio, QGIS, and rigorous experimental design to ensure that research outputs are reproducible, data-driven, and suitable for publication.
With more than four peer-reviewed publications in plant protection, soil-borne pathogens, agroforestry, and climate-resilient farming, my work consistently bridges the gap between laboratory discovery and field-level application, the critical interface where food security is either protected or compromised. I was awarded the emerging visionary award for my impactful research findings in the 3rd International Poster Competition for Young Researchers.
Beyond research, I have been recognized as a Star Performer in the Grant Thornton ESG Benchmarking Program and as a Promising Intern at ORIYET, experiences that strengthened my commitment to precision, accountability, and interdisciplinary collaboration.
My next goal is to pursue a PhD where I can expand my expertise in molecular plant–microbe interactions, disease resistance mechanisms, and precision crop protection technologies. I aim to contribute to research that advances sustainable agriculture and strengthens the resilience of global food systems.
